passage: "You're up again?" Ritu found her sister Kalyani on the balcony at 3:40 am. "It was 3:33 when I woke up. Third time this month. And every time, something goes wrong the next day." "Like what?" "The bus broke down. Amma's knee hurt. The laptop crashed." Ritu sat down. "Didi, things go wrong most days." Kalyani laughed weakly. "I know. That's what I keep telling myself. So here's my plan. For two weeks I'll write down every time I wake up, whatever the time, and whether the next day is bad." "And if it's the same with 2:10 or 4:50?" "Then it's just me noticing the scary number." Kalyani pulled her shawl tighter. "And if it keeps frightening me like this, I'll book the counsellor at work. I don't want to lie awake counting." "I'll remind you," said Ritu.

passage: I'm Preeti, and last spring I became convinced my manager, Vijay, was watching my screen. Every time I opened a job site on my lunch break, an email from him seemed to land within minutes. It happened on Monday. Then Wednesday. My stomach dropped each time. I started closing tabs and jumping at notification sounds. One evening I made myself ask: what would this look like if it were just chance? He sends dozens of emails a day. So for two weeks I noted every time I opened the site and every email from him, matched or not. Twenty-six emails. Four near my breaks. The rest came at any time at all. That helped. But I was still tense, still scanning for signs, and it was wearing me out. So I booked a session with a counsellor. Talking it through helped more than any spreadsheet.

qa.q: How many emails from Vijay did Preeti count, and how many came near the breaks?
qa.a: Twenty-six emails, and four came near the breaks.

qa.q: How was Preeti feeling during those weeks, and what shows it?
qa.a: Anxious and on edge 😰 Preeti's stomach dropped each time, and Preeti kept closing tabs and jumping at notification sounds.

qa.q: What two steps did Preeti take, and why did both matter?
qa.a: Preeti tested the pattern against chance for two weeks, then booked a counsellor when the tension kept wearing on, because the numbers alone did not ease the worry.

qa.q: How might Vijay have been affected if Preeti had acted on the belief without testing it?
qa.a: Vijay could have been treated with suspicion or accused of spying over emails that were simply part of an ordinary busy day.

grounding: An adult tests a worrying pattern against chance and, when the pattern-hunting keeps wearing on, sees a counsellor.

passage: Supervisor's note, analytics team. Jagdish. Afreen, 24, came to me on Tuesday, excited. In last quarter's data, customer complaints seemed to jump every time our radio advert played. She had a chart ready. Before presenting it, though, she did two things I want to record. First, she asked, "What would this look like if it were just luck?" and shuffled the advert dates randomly a hundred times; similar jumps turned up in about a third of the shuffles. Second, she waited for this month's data as a fresh test. The link vanished. She was disappointed, and said so, but she binned the chart. She also told me that late nights staring at charts had left her jittery, seeing links in everything, so she has booked a session with the company counsellor. I told her both were good decisions.

qa.q: What did Afreen do with the advert dates?
qa.a: She shuffled them randomly a hundred times.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel when the link vanished in this month's data?
qa.a: Disappointed, and she said so, yet she still binned the chart.

qa.q: Why was waiting for this month's data a wise step before presenting?
qa.a: It tested the pattern on data it had not been drawn from, and when the link vanished it showed the jumps were likely chance.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have been affected if Afreen had presented the first chart?
qa.a: They might have changed or blamed the radio advert based on a chance pattern, wasting time and money.

grounding: A supervisor records how a young analyst tested a pattern against chance and new data, and booked a counsellor when pattern-hunting left her jittery.

passage:
Wednesday night

For three weeks I've been reading number plates. If I see a plate ending in 13 on the way to the office, something goes wrong that day. A missed bus, a bad meeting, a cold lunch. It started as a joke. Lately it isn't funny. I scan every car. I've started taking longer routes to avoid the parking lot.
Tonight I tried something Mahima suggested. What would it look like if it were just chance? I went back through my notes. On days with no 13, things went wrong too. About as often. So the pattern is me, looking.
But the scanning won't switch off, and it's making me anxious. Mahima says that's worth talking about with someone, not just my diary. I've booked a session with the office counsellor for Friday.
Deepak

qa.q: What number did Deepak think signalled a bad day?
qa.a: A number plate ending in 13.

qa.q: How does Deepak seem to feel about the scanning now?
qa.a: Deepak is anxious and tired of it, since it has stopped being a joke and won't switch off.

qa.q: Which steps in Deepak's approach are wise, and why?
qa.a: Checking days without 13 against days with it tested the pattern against chance, and booking the counsellor gets help for the anxiety the checking can't fix.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel about Deepak booking the session?
qa.a: Mahima would likely feel relieved and supportive, glad that the worry won't be carried alone.

grounding: An adult tests a feared pattern against chance and seeks a counsellor as the pattern-hunting becomes distressing.
